intro: This unit has stories of people who needed help. Hagar was alone in the desert. Moses was far from home. Mary heard surprising news. In each story, the Bible says a messenger from God came close and spoke kindly.

Then come stories about Jesus. He fed hungry people and welcomed children. He sent his friends to all nations. At Pentecost, people heard good news in their own languages. Michael Heiser, a teacher who read the Bible's old languages, saw an invitation for every nation.

In this unit you will retell these stories in order. You will learn words like messenger, holy and nation. You will say what Heiser thought and what other readers think. And you will find ways to help others feel welcome.
bigQuestion: In the Bible stories, how does God come close and invite everyone home?

timeline.t: Hagar is sad and runs into the desert (Genesis 16)
The Angel of the LORD finds Hagar by a spring
Moses watches sheep and sees a burning bush (Exodus 3)
God tells Moses he will help his people
Jesus feeds hungry people and welcomes children (Mark 6 and 10)
Jesus calms the wind and the waves (Mark 4)
Jesus sends his friends to all nations (Matthew 28:19)
At Pentecost, people hear in their own languages (Acts 2)
A crowd from every nation stands together (Revelation 7:9)

words.d: someone who brings words or news from someone else
a special messenger in the Bible stories who speaks for God
special and set apart for God
God's helpers in heaven in the Bible stories; many bring messages
a big group of people with their own land, leaders and often their own language
a Jewish harvest holiday; in Acts 2, the day Jesus' friends spoke in many languages
the different sets of words people use to talk, like English and Spanish
to greet someone gladly and help them feel they belong

test.q: Who met the Angel of the LORD by a spring in the desert?
test.why: Genesis 16 tells how the Angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring.

test.q: What did Moses see in Exodus 3?
choices: A bush that burned but did not burn up
test.why: Exodus 3 says Moses saw a bush that burned but was not burned up.

test.q: What did Heiser think about the Angel of the LORD?
choices: He was God himself, coming close
He was just a bright light
test.why: Heiser thought the Angel of the LORD was God himself, coming close so people could see.

test.q: Which angel brought good news to Mary?
test.why: Luke 1 says the angel Gabriel came to Mary.

test.q: What do angels often say in the stories?
test.why: In Luke, angels often say, "Do not be afraid."

choices: Special and set apart for God
test.why: Holy means special and set apart for God, like the ground by the bush.

test.q: In Matthew 28:19, where did Jesus send his friends?
test.why: Jesus sent his friends to all nations.

test.q: At Pentecost, how did the visitors hear the good news?
test.why: Acts 2 says each visitor heard in their own language.

test.q: Heiser saw Pentecost as the opposite of which story?
test.why: At Babel, languages sent people apart. Heiser saw Pentecost bringing them together.

choices: A crowd from every nation, all together
test.why: Revelation 7:9 pictures a crowd from every nation and language, standing together.

write.prompt: Pick two stories: Hagar (Genesis 16), Moses (Exodus 3), or Pentecost (Acts 2). Draw or tell what happened. Who came close? Who was welcomed? Say what Heiser thought.
tips: Name the book, like Genesis or Acts.
Tell the story in order: first, next, last.
Use one unit word, like messenger, holy or nation.

title: Everyone Invited Home

chapters.title: The Messenger Who Came Close
chapters.bigQuestion: In the Bible stories, how did God come close to people who needed help?

story.title: The Bush That Did Not Burn Up
story.kicker: Moses is watching sheep. Then he sees something new. A bush is on fire, but it stays green.
paragraphs: This story is in the Bible, in a book called Exodus. Moses lives in the dry hills. He takes care of sheep. Each day he walks with them. He finds them grass and water. It is quiet work.
One day Moses looks up. He sees a bush on a hill. The bush has fire in it! But the leaves stay green. The branches do not turn black. The bush keeps burning, and it does not burn up.
Moses walks closer to look. The story says a voice calls from the bush. "Moses, Moses!" Moses answers, "Here I am." The voice tells him to take off his sandals. This place is special, the voice says.
The story says it was God who spoke from the bush. God had heard his people crying in Egypt. God would help them. And God wanted Moses to help too. Moses listened carefully.
story.think: Moses walked closer to look at something new. What do you do when you see something new?

lessons.title: Hagar by the Spring
lessons.mainIdea: In Genesis 16, the Angel of the LORD found Hagar in the desert and spoke kindly to her.
reading: This story is in Genesis 16. A woman named Hagar was sad. Life at home was hard for her. So she ran away into the desert. The desert was hot and dry.
Hagar stopped by a spring of water. The story says a special *messenger* found her there. The Bible calls him the *Angel of the LORD*. He asked her, "Where are you going?"
The messenger listened to Hagar. He told her she would have a baby boy. The boy would be named Ishmael. That name means "God hears." The story says God had heard Hagar.

words.d: someone who brings words or news from someone else
a special messenger in the Bible stories who speaks for God

look.title: At the Spring
look.text: The Angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring in the desert. He asked where she came from and where she was going. He told her she would have a son. He said to name him Ishmael, because the LORD had heard her.
look.cite: Genesis 16:7–11, retold in simple words from the World English Bible
look.prompt: Where was Hagar when the messenger found her?

check.q: Where did the messenger find Hagar?
choices: By a spring in the desert
check.why: Genesis 16 says the Angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert.

check.q: What does the name Ishmael mean?
check.why: Ishmael means "God hears." The story says God had heard Hagar.

check.q: What is a messenger?
choices: Someone who brings words from someone else
check.why: A messenger brings words or news from someone else.

lessons.title: The God Who Sees
lessons.mainIdea: Hagar gave God a name that means the God who sees me.
reading: Hagar felt alone in the desert. Then the messenger came. He knew her name. He knew she was sad. He talked with her gently.
Hagar thought about what happened. Then she gave God a *name*. In Genesis 16:13 she calls him "the God who sees me." She felt seen and cared for.
Hagar went back home. Later her baby boy was born. She named him Ishmael, just as the messenger said. The story ends with a promise kept.

words.d: a word that tells who someone is; in the Bible, a name can tell about a person

look.title: Someone Sees You
look.text: Look at a boy on the playground. He is sitting by the fence. He feels left out. A teacher sees him. She walks over. She sits down next to him. She says his name softly.
look.prompt: How do you think the boy feels when the teacher sees him and says his name?

check.q: What name did Hagar give God?
check.why: In Genesis 16:13, Hagar calls God "the God who sees me."

check.q: How did Hagar feel before the messenger came?
check.why: Hagar ran away because she was sad. In the desert she felt alone.

check.q: What did Hagar name her baby boy?
check.why: She named him Ishmael, just as the messenger said.

lessons.title: Moses Sees a Bush
lessons.mainIdea: In Exodus 3, the Angel of the LORD came to Moses in a bush that burned but did not burn up.
reading: This story is in Exodus 3. Moses was watching sheep near a mountain. The Bible calls the mountain Horeb. It was a quiet day.
The story says the Angel of the LORD came to Moses in a *flame* of fire. The fire was in a *bush*. The bush burned. But it did not burn up.
Moses said, "I will go and look." He wanted to know why the bush stayed green. Moses was curious. He walked closer.

words.d: the bright, hot part of a fire
a small plant with many branches, smaller than a tree

look.title: The Burning Bush
look.text: Moses was keeping sheep near the mountain of God. The Angel of the LORD came to him in a flame of fire in the middle of a bush. Moses looked. The bush was burning, but it was not burned up. Moses said he would go closer and see.
look.cite: Exodus 3:1–3, retold in simple words from the World English Bible
look.prompt: What was strange about the bush?

check.q: What was Moses doing when he saw the bush?
check.why: Exodus 3 says Moses was taking care of sheep near a mountain.

check.q: What was strange about the bush?
choices: It burned but did not burn up
check.why: The story says the bush burned, but it was not burned up.

check.q: Who came to Moses in the flame, the story says?
check.why: Exodus 3:2 says the Angel of the LORD came to Moses in a flame of fire.

lessons.title: A Special Place
lessons.mainIdea: The story says God spoke from the bush and told Moses he would help his people.
reading: Moses came near the bush. The story says God called, "Moses, Moses!" Moses said, "Here I am." He was ready to listen.
God told Moses to take off his sandals. The ground there was *holy*. Holy means special and set apart for God. Moses covered his face.
Then God said he had seen his people in Egypt. They were working hard and hurting. God had heard them cry. The story says God would bring them out, and Moses would help.

words.d: special and set apart for God

look.title: Moses Grows Up
rows: Age when he talked to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7)
look.cite: Acts 7:23–30 and Exodus 7:7, World English Bible
look.prompt: How many years did Moses watch sheep before he saw the bush?

check.q: What did God tell Moses to take off?
check.why: In Exodus 3:5, God tells Moses to take off his sandals because the ground is holy.

check.q: What does holy mean?
choices: Special and set apart for God
check.why: Holy means special and set apart for God.

check.q: Who had God heard crying, the story says?
check.why: Exodus 3 says God heard his people crying in Egypt and would help them.

lessons.title: Who Was the Messenger?
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser thought the Angel of the LORD was God himself, coming close so people could see him.
reading: In Exodus 3, the Angel of the LORD is in the bush. Then God speaks from the same bush. So who was there? People have asked this for a very long time.
Michael Heiser was a Bible teacher. He read the Bible in its old languages. He thought the Angel of the LORD was God himself. God came close, Heiser said. People could *see* him.
Other readers think a little differently. They think the Angel was a messenger God sent. He spoke God's words for God. Both groups read the same story closely.

words.d: to look at something with your eyes

look.title: Heiser's Idea
look.text: Heiser noticed that in some stories the Angel of the LORD speaks as God, and people say they have seen God. He thought this messenger was God himself, showing up in a form people could see.
look.cite: Idea from Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015), in our own words
look.prompt: What did Heiser think about the Angel of the LORD?

check.q: What did Heiser think the Angel of the LORD was?
choices: God himself, coming close so people could see
check.why: Heiser thought the Angel of the LORD was God himself, coming close in a way people could see.

check.q: What do some other readers think?
choices: The Angel was a messenger God sent to speak for him
check.why: Other readers think the Angel was a messenger sent by God, speaking God's words.

check.q: Who was Michael Heiser?
choices: A teacher who read the Bible in its old languages
check.why: Heiser was a teacher who studied the Bible in its old languages.

sections.title: Good News, Do Not Be Afraid

lessons.title: Gabriel Visits Mary
lessons.mainIdea: In Luke 1, the angel Gabriel brought Mary good news about a baby named Jesus.
reading: The Bible tells about *angels* too. Angels are God's helpers in heaven. They often carry messages. One angel has a name. His name is *Gabriel*.
This story is in Luke 1. Gabriel came to a young woman named Mary. She lived in a town called Nazareth. At first Mary was surprised. Gabriel said, "Do not be afraid."
Then Gabriel told Mary good news. She would have a baby boy. She should name him Jesus. Mary listened. She said yes.

words.d: God's helpers in heaven in the Bible stories; many bring messages
an angel named in the Bible who brought good news to Mary

look.title: Gabriel's Good News
look.text: The angel Gabriel was sent to a town called Nazareth. He came to Mary. He told her not to be afraid. He said she would have a son, and she should call him Jesus.
look.cite: Luke 1:26–31, retold in simple words from the World English Bible
look.prompt: What were Gabriel's first kind words to Mary?

check.q: Which angel came to Mary?
check.why: Luke 1 says the angel Gabriel came to Mary in Nazareth.

check.q: What did Gabriel say first to help Mary?
check.why: Gabriel told Mary, "Do not be afraid."

check.q: What name did Gabriel give for the baby?
check.why: Gabriel told Mary to name her son Jesus.

lessons.title: What Helps Us Feel Safe
lessons.mainIdea: In the stories, angels often say "Do not be afraid," and the stories say God is near.
reading: Look back at the stories. Hagar was sad. Moses was surprised. Mary was surprised too. Each time, the messenger was kind and *calm*.
In Luke, angels say "Do not be afraid" again and again. The stories say God is near. They say God cares. Many people feel calm when they hear them.
Feeling scared or new is okay. Some things help us feel *safe*. A grown-up we trust. A quiet place. A slow, deep breath. You can ask for help.

words.d: quiet and steady inside
protected and cared for, not in danger

look.title: A Calm Corner
look.text: Look at the corner of a classroom. There is a soft rug. There is a pillow. There is a small plant. A girl sits there. She breathes in slowly. She breathes out slowly. Her body feels calm.
look.prompt: What helps you feel calm and safe? Name one thing.

check.q: What do angels often say in the stories?
check.why: In Luke, angels often say, "Do not be afraid."

check.q: What is one thing that can help you feel safe?
check.why: A grown-up you trust can help you feel safe. You can ask for help.

check.q: How were the messengers in these stories?
check.why: With Hagar, Moses and Mary, the messengers were kind and calm.

review.q: Which book tells about Moses and the burning bush?
review.why: The burning bush story is in Exodus 3.

review.q: Which book tells about Hagar and the spring?
Which book tells about Gabriel and Mary?
review.why: Gabriel's visit to Mary is in Luke 1.

review.q: What does the Angel of the LORD do in these stories?
choices: He speaks for God and helps people
review.why: In Genesis 16 and Exodus 3, the Angel of the LORD speaks for God and helps.

review.q: Heiser thought the Angel of the LORD was who?
review.why: Heiser thought the Angel of the LORD was God himself, coming close so people could see.

review.q: Hagar called God a name. What did it mean?
review.why: In Genesis 16:13, Hagar calls God "the God who sees me."

chapters.title: Good News for Every Nation
chapters.bigQuestion: In the Bible stories, who is invited into God's family?

story.title: Hello in a New Language
story.kicker: A new student joins the class. He speaks Spanish. Soon the whole class can say hello to him.
paragraphs: It is Monday at a school in Chicago. A new boy stands at the door. His name is Mateo. He just moved from far away. Mateo speaks Spanish. He knows only a few English words.
The teacher smiles. She says, "Mateo, welcome!" Then she turns to the class. "How do we say hello in Spanish?" Mateo says it softly. "Hola." The class tries it together. "Hola, Mateo!"
At lunch, Ava saves Mateo a seat. She points to her apple. She says, "Apple." Mateo points too. He says, "Manzana." They both laugh. Now each one knows a new word.
By Friday, Mateo has three friends. The class knows five Spanish words. Mateo knows ten new English words. Two languages, one class. Everyone belongs.
story.think: How did the class help Mateo feel welcome? What could you do for a new friend?

lessons.title: Jesus Helped Hurting People
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels tell how Jesus fed hungry people and welcomed children.
reading: The *Gospels* are four books in the Bible. They tell about Jesus. One story is in Mark 6. A big crowd came to hear Jesus. It got late. The people were hungry.
Jesus' friends found five loaves of bread and two fish. Jesus thanked God. His friends passed out the food. The story says everyone ate and was full.
Another story is in Mark 10. Parents brought their children to Jesus. His friends tried to send them away. Jesus said, "Let the children come to me." He hugged them and *blessed* them.

words.d: the four books in the Bible that tell about Jesus: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John
said kind, good words over someone and asked God to be good to them

look.title: Five Loaves, Two Fish
look.text: Look at the grassy hill. Many families sit in groups. Children are tired. Their tummies rumble. A basket comes by. It has bread and fish. A girl takes some. She passes the basket on. Everyone gets some.
look.prompt: How do you think the hungry families felt when the food came?

check.q: How much food did Jesus' friends find in Mark 6?
check.why: Mark 6 says there were five loaves of bread and two fish.

check.q: What did Jesus say about the children in Mark 10?
choices: Let the children come to me
check.why: Jesus said, "Let the children come to me," and he blessed them.

check.q: What are the Gospels?
choices: Four books that tell about Jesus
check.why: The Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. They tell about Jesus.

lessons.title: Stronger Than Every Bad Power
lessons.mainIdea: The stories say Jesus was stronger than every bad power, even the wind and the waves.
reading: This story is in Mark 4. Jesus and his friends were in a boat. A big wind came. Waves splashed in. His friends were scared. Jesus was asleep.
They woke him up. Jesus spoke to the wind and the sea. He said, "Peace, be still." The wind stopped. The water became calm. His friends asked, "Who is this?"
The Gospels say Jesus was *stronger* than every bad power. Bad powers had to listen to him. Heiser thought about why Jesus came. He said Jesus came to bring every *nation* back to God's family.

words.d: having more power than someone or something else
a big group of people with their own land, leaders and often their own language

look.title: Peace, Be Still
look.text: A great storm of wind came, and waves beat into the boat. Jesus woke up. He told the wind to stop, and he said to the sea, "Peace, be still." The wind stopped, and there was a great calm.
look.cite: Mark 4:37–39, retold in simple words from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What happened after Jesus spoke to the wind and the sea?

check.q: Where were Jesus and his friends when the wind came?
check.why: Mark 4 says they were in a boat when the storm came.

check.q: What did Jesus say to the sea?
check.why: The story says Jesus told the sea, "Peace, be still," and it became calm.

check.q: What did Heiser think Jesus came to do?
choices: Bring every nation back into God's family
check.why: Heiser thought Jesus came to bring every nation back into God's family.

lessons.title: Go to All Nations
lessons.mainIdea: In Matthew 28:19, Jesus sent his friends to all nations.
reading: This is near the end of the book of Matthew. Jesus met his friends on a mountain. He had a big job for them.
In Matthew 28:19, Jesus told them to go to all *nations*. Not just one land. Not just one people. All of them. They should teach people and welcome them.
Think back to Babel in Genesis 11. The people spread out then. They became many nations. Now Jesus sent his friends to every one of them.

words.d: big groups of people, each with their own land and often their own language

look.title: A Map of the World
look.text: Look at a big map on the classroom wall. It shows many lands. Some are blue with lakes. Some are green with forests. Some are yellow with deserts. Each land has people. Each has its own words.
look.prompt: Jesus said to go to all nations. Point to three places on a map. Who lives there?

check.q: Where did Jesus send his friends in Matthew 28:19?
check.why: In Matthew 28:19, Jesus told his friends to go to all nations.

check.q: Which story told how people spread out into many nations?
check.why: At Babel in Genesis 11, people were spread out into many nations.

check.q: What is a nation?
choices: A big group of people with their own land
check.why: A nation is a big group of people. It has its own land and often its own language.

lessons.title: Pentecost: Many Languages
lessons.mainIdea: At Pentecost, people from many lands heard the good news in their own languages.
reading: This story is in Acts 2. Jesus' friends were together in Jerusalem. It was a holiday called *Pentecost*. People had come from many lands.
The story says a sound came like a strong wind. Something like little flames rested on each friend. Then the friends began to speak in other *languages*.
A crowd came running. The visitors were amazed. Each one heard the friends in their own language! They heard about God's great works.

words.d: a Jewish harvest holiday; in Acts 2, the day Jesus' friends spoke in many languages
the different sets of words people use to talk, like English and Spanish

look.title: Each in Their Own Language
look.text: When the crowd heard the sound, they came together. They were amazed, because each one heard the friends speaking in their own language. They asked how this could be.
look.cite: Acts 2:6–8, retold in simple words from the World English Bible

check.q: Which book tells the Pentecost story?
check.why: The Pentecost story is in Acts 2.

check.q: What rested on each friend, the story says?
check.why: Acts 2 says something like little flames rested on each of them.

check.q: Why was the crowd amazed?
choices: Each one heard their own language
check.why: Each visitor heard the friends speaking in their own language.

lessons.title: Babel Turned Around
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser saw Pentecost as the opposite of Babel: languages brought people together again.
reading: Remember Babel? In Genesis 11, God mixed up the people's languages. They could not understand each other. They spread out over the earth.
Heiser saw Pentecost as the *opposite* of Babel. At Babel, many languages sent people apart. At Pentecost, many languages brought people together to hear good news.
Other readers say Pentecost is mostly about God's Spirit. The Spirit came to Jesus' friends. Heiser saw that too. He also saw all nations invited back.

words.d: as different as can be, like up and down

look.title: A Small Group Grows
look.cite: Acts 1:15 and Acts 2:41, World English Bible
look.prompt: Which number is biggest? What does it tell about Pentecost?

check.q: What did Heiser say Pentecost was like?
check.why: Heiser saw Pentecost as the opposite of Babel.

check.q: At Babel, what did the many languages do?
check.why: At Babel, people could not understand each other, so they spread apart.

check.q: About how many people joined at Pentecost, Acts 2:41 says?
check.why: Acts 2:41 says about 3,000 people joined that day.

lessons.title: A Crowd From Every Nation
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 7:9 pictures a huge crowd from every nation and language, all together.
reading: The last book in the Bible is *Revelation*. It is full of pictures in words. One picture is in Revelation 7:9.
John, the writer, sees a huge crowd. It is so big no one can count it. The people come from every nation. They speak every language. They all stand together before God.
The people wear white clothes. They hold palm branches, like at a happy parade. Many readers see this as the end of the big story. Every nation is invited home to God's family.

words.d: the last book in the Bible; it uses word pictures about the future

look.title: A Crowd No One Could Count
look.text: John looked and saw a great crowd that no one could count. They came from every nation, every family group, every people and every language. They stood before God's throne, dressed in white, with palm branches in their hands.
look.cite: Revelation 7:9, retold in simple words from the World English Bible
look.prompt: Where did the people in the crowd come from?

check.q: Which book has the huge crowd from every nation?
check.why: Revelation 7:9 pictures the huge crowd from every nation.

check.q: What did the people in the crowd hold?
check.why: Revelation 7:9 says they held palm branches.

check.q: How big was the crowd?
choices: So big no one could count it
check.why: The story says the crowd was so big that no one could count it.

lessons.title: Making Room for Others
lessons.mainIdea: The stories invite everyone in, and we can welcome people who are new or different.
reading: Look at the stories in this chapter. Jesus fed hungry people. He welcomed children. At Pentecost, every language was heard. In Revelation, every nation is together.
Many Christians read these stories as an invitation. Everyone is *welcome* in God's family, they say. Heiser taught this too.
You can make room for others. Learn how to say hello in a new language. Save a seat. Share a toy. Say someone's name kindly. Small things help a lot.

words.d: to greet someone gladly and help them feel they belong

look.title: Hello Around the World
look.text: Look at the chart on the classroom door. It says hello in many languages. Hola is Spanish. Bonjour is French. Jambo is Swahili. Ni hao is Chinese. Each morning, the class picks one to say.
look.prompt: Which hello would you like to learn? Who could you say it to?

check.q: What is one way to welcome a new friend?
check.why: Saving a seat helps a new friend feel they belong.

check.q: What does welcome mean?
check.why: To welcome is to greet someone gladly and help them feel they belong.

check.q: How do many Christians read these stories?
choices: As a story about a tower
check.why: Many Christians read these stories as an invitation. Everyone is welcome, they say.

review.q: Where did Jesus send his friends in Matthew 28:19?
review.why: In Matthew 28:19, Jesus sent his friends to all nations.

review.q: What happened at Pentecost in Acts 2?
choices: People heard good news in their own languages
A big boat floated on water
A bush burned but did not burn up
review.why: At Pentecost, people from many lands heard the friends in their own languages.

review.q: Heiser saw Pentecost as the opposite of what?
review.why: Heiser saw Pentecost as the opposite of Babel, where languages sent people apart.

review.q: In Mark 4, what did the wind and waves do when Jesus spoke?
review.why: Mark 4 says the wind stopped and there was a great calm.
Revelation 7:9 pictures a crowd from every nation and language.

review.q: What did Jesus do for the children in Mark 10?
review.why: Jesus said to let the children come, and he blessed them.
